title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 36
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Stitch That Could Be Made by Machine
passages.text:
A. Sewing resisted mechanisation for longer than spinning or weaving, and the reason is instructive. Thread and cloth could be made by machines decades before anyone could build one that joined cloth together, because hand sewing passes a single thread completely through the fabric and back, and no mechanism can pass a needle right through and retrieve it efficiently. The problem was not power or precision but the geometry of the stitch itself.

B. The solution was to abandon the hand stitch rather than to imitate it. A needle with the eye at its point, carrying thread only partway through, combined with a second thread supplied from below to lock each loop, produces a join that no hand sewer would make and that a machine can make continuously. Mechanisation succeeded here by changing the product slightly, which is a pattern visible in many technologies described as automating an existing task.

C. The machine's immediate effect was not on factories but on households. It was sold to domestic purchasers on instalment terms — an innovation in selling as significant as the device — and the labour it saved was unpaid labour, since clothing a family was work done at home and mostly by women. Time released in this way does not appear in any economic statistic of the period, which is part of why the machine's importance was long understated.

D. The factory consequences arrived with the division of the work rather than with the machine alone. Once garment assembly could be broken into repeated operations, each performed on a machine by a worker who did only that, output per person rose sharply and the skill required per worker fell. The industry that resulted was labour-intensive, low-capital and mobile, and those three properties have determined its geography ever since.

E. That mobility is the industry's defining economic feature. A garment factory can be established with modest investment and relocated when wages rise, so production has migrated repeatedly towards lower-cost regions and will continue to; the same characteristics that let a poor country enter manufacturing let the industry leave when the country becomes less poor. Garment work has been the entry point to industrialisation for a long succession of economies precisely because it is easy to lose.

F. Automation has repeatedly been predicted and repeatedly failed to arrive, for a reason the first paragraph anticipates. Rigid materials are easy for machines to handle and limp fabric is not: cloth deforms unpredictably when gripped, and reliably positioning a soft, sliding, three-dimensional assembly remains beyond most equipment. The stitch was mechanised in the nineteenth century; the handling of cloth largely has not been.

passages.title: Shutting Down for Winter
passages.text:
Hibernation is not sleep, and treating it as a long version of sleep obscures what is actually happening. An animal in deep hibernation has a body temperature within a few degrees of its surroundings, a heart rate reduced to a small fraction of normal, and a metabolic rate low enough that months can pass on stored fat. Sleep is a neurological state; hibernation is a controlled shutdown of the machinery that maintains body temperature at all.

The saving is enormous and the strategy is nonetheless not universal, which tells you it carries costs. Rewarming from deep torpor is expensive, and hibernating animals do it repeatedly through the winter rather than once at the end — brief arousals to normal temperature that consume a substantial share of the entire winter's energy budget. Why they occur is not settled; the leading suggestions involve immune function, waste clearance and the maintenance of neural connections, none yet demonstrated conclusively.

Preparation is a physiological reorganisation rather than simply eating more. The composition of stored fat changes, since fats that stay fluid at low temperature are required for membranes to function near freezing; the gut is remodelled; and in some species the timing is driven by an internal annual clock that persists even in animals kept in constant conditions with unlimited food. The animal is not responding to cold so much as anticipating it.

Not all of what is called hibernation is the same phenomenon. Bears reduce metabolism substantially while maintaining a body temperature far above their surroundings, do not become fully torpid, and can rouse quickly — a different and in some ways more remarkable arrangement, since they go months without eating, drinking or excreting while retaining muscle and bone that inactivity should waste. Small hibernators become cold; large ones mostly do not.

Torpor is also not confined to winter or to mammals of cold regions. Many small birds and mammals drop their temperature overnight to save energy, some desert species become torpid in response to heat and drought rather than cold, and the capacity appears scattered across the animal kingdom in a pattern suggesting it is ancient and repeatedly lost rather than repeatedly invented.

Medical interest in these mechanisms is genuine and the most-repeated version of it is misleading. That bears retain bone and muscle through months of immobility, and that hibernators tolerate body temperatures and blood flows that would injure a human, are facts worth understanding for what they might teach about tissue protection. Inducing anything resembling hibernation in humans is not a current capability, and the induced cooling used in some emergency medicine is a much smaller and different intervention.

passages.title: Why the Restaurant Closed
passages.text:
Restaurants fail at rates that would be considered a crisis in most industries and are treated as a normal condition of this one. The figure most often quoted — a large majority closing within a few years — is inflated by counting ownership changes and relocations as failures, but the corrected rate remains high. What makes the business unusually hard is a combination of features that individually appear in other industries and rarely appear together.

Perishability is the first. Ingredients decay, so inventory must be bought against a forecast of demand that cannot be verified until the evening; a quiet night converts stock into waste, and a busy one converts customers into disappointment. Nothing can be stored between the two, and no other retail business has both a perishable input and a product that must be manufactured within minutes of being ordered.

Fixed costs arrive whether anyone comes or not. Rent, equipment finance and a minimum staffing level are committed before the first customer, and the margin on each additional meal is high while the margin across the business is thin — which means the difference between a profitable restaurant and a closing one is often a small difference in how full it is. Occupancy, not price or quality, is usually the variable that decides.

Labour presents a structural difficulty that improved management does not remove. The work is required in concentrated bursts at unsociable hours, cannot be relocated or deferred, and is paid at rates the price of the food will support rather than what the hours deserve. High turnover follows, turnover degrades the consistency that brings customers back, and the resulting instability is a symptom of the economics rather than of poor employers.

Delivery platforms have altered the arithmetic in ways that took time to become visible. They supply demand a restaurant could not reach and take a commission that frequently exceeds the entire margin on the order, so volume rises while profit does not; and because the platform holds the customer relationship, a restaurant that grows through it has grown a business it does not own. Several operators have concluded that the profitable response is to serve fewer orders.

The reason the failure rate persists is partly that the barriers to entry are low and the appeal is high. Opening a restaurant requires less capital than most businesses and attracts people motivated by the food rather than by the arithmetic, so new entrants replace the failures continuously and the average returns stay poor. It is an industry with a permanent oversupply of willing participants, which is pleasant for customers and unforgiving for owners.
